News & Politics

Boelter had previously pleaded not guilty in last year’s fatal shooting of Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and an armed attack on another lawmaker and his family. He’s set to appear in court Thursday morning.

By Sarah Nelson and

Jeff Day

Vance Boelter, the man charged in the shootings of two Minnesota lawmakers and their families last summer, is expected to plead guilty in his federal murder case, according to a court record filed Wednesday and two sources familiar with the case.

The change comes after the Justice Department revealed it would not seek the death penalty against Boelter, 58, in the attacks last summer that jarred the state. A memo filed Wednesday by Minnesota’s U.S. Attorney’s Office suggests the decision not to seek a death sentence against Boelter was made “in accordance with the terms delineated in a proposed plea agreement.”

Boelter pleaded not guilty last year to his six federal offenses tied to the shootings that killed Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and injured Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, and their daughter, Hope.

The plea hearing in Boelter’s federal case is scheduled for 10 a.m. Thursday in a Minneapolis courtroom before U.S. District Judge John Tunheim.

A source familiar with the hearing said Boelter is expected to enter a guilty plea related to his federal charges of killing the Hortmans and attempting to kill the Hoffmans.

Boelter is not expected to receive any leniency in exchange for his plea, said a second source familiar with the proceedings.

Boelter’s federal case has remained in the early stages since his indictment and no trial date had been set. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster expressed frustration during a hearing in April over how long it took prosecutors to decide whether they would seek the death penalty against him.

According to his indictment, Boelter disguised himself as a police officer when he arrived at the lawmakers’ homes in the middle of the night on June 14. He was arrested near his home in Green Isle, Minn., after the largest manhunt in state history.

The first two counts against Boelter allege that he stalked the Hortmans and Hoffmans through the use of interstate facilities, namely the internet. Prosecutors argued that stalking his victims rose to a crime of violence. Ultimately, the Justice Department said it agreed with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota that a conviction for interstate stalking is not eligible for the death penalty.

A similar decision was made in January by a federal judge in the case against Luigi Mangione. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett in New York dismissed a nearly identical federal murder charge against Mangione in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

Boelter also faces charges in Hennepin County District Court that include two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of first-degree attempted murder, including against Rep. Kristin Bahner, whose home he allegedly visited that night while she was out of town. He also faces one count of animal cruelty against the the Hortmans’ dog, Gilbert, who was shot and had to be euthanized, and one count of impersonating a police officer.

Immediately after his arrest, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty requested to prosecute the state’s murder charges before the federal case but was denied.

Boelter was on the run for 43 hours after shooting the Hoffmans at 2:02 a.m. in the early morning hours of June 14. He interacted with local police officers twice after that, first in New Hope outside the home of Sen. Ann Rest at 2:36 a.m. and again at 3:35 a.m. outside the Hortman home. Brooklyn Park officers fired shots at Boelter as he killed Mark Hortman in the doorway of the home. Boelter proceeded to kill Melissa Hortman before escaping.

The lack of a coordinated response by several law enforcement agencies, including the State Patrol which is charged with protecting state lawmakers, has come under question since the attacks.

Last fall, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, Minnesota State Patrol, Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office, and the police departments of Brooklyn Park, Champlin and New Hope agreed to pay $429,500 for an independent review of the law enforcement response to the shootings.

Paul Walsh of the Minnesota Star Tribune contributed to this story.
